tasks.notes:
## Goal
Complete the implementation of `commands/por-prep.ts` to have it:
- iterate through all `*.md` files in the prep folder
- for each file found:
	- read the file contents and split it into "header sections": a top-level H1 header (in Markdown, i.e. `# title text`) + all lines below it up to either (a) the next top-level H1, or (b) the EOF.
	- for each header section in which the title text (=header text) ends with an exclamation mark `!` , do these sequentially:
		1. create a GitHub issue (via `useGitHub()`) such that:
			- the title text *w/o the exclamation mark* becomes the issue title
			- the non-title lines of the header section become the issue body (retaining all Markdown formatting as-is)
			- the issue gets assigned to *all* configured `assignees`
			- the issue gets connected to the project with its status field set to the configured `initialStatus`
			- for each `#tag` within the title (hashtag sign `#` + any sequence of non-whitespace characters), compare *tag*  to the set of known GitHub labels (per `GitHub`'s `labels` getter) - if there's a match, assign that label to the newly created issue
		2. remove the entire header section from the Markdown file and instead append it to `.done.md` in the prep folder (create if missing)
		3. store the modified contents back to both Markdown files *before* moving on to the next header section
## Notes
- the `GitHub` instance already maintains persisted data on the GitHub project setup. Reuse it or extend that system rather than coming up with ad-hoc solutions - e.g. add class methods `createIssue()`, `setIssueStatus()` etc. and invoke them from the command script

	2. between 2 consequent invocations, at least 5 seconds must have passed

Opinionated task and context management for [Orca ADE](https://www.onorca.dev/) using [Obsidian](https://obsidian.md/) and GitHub labels.

## Setup
### Step 1: Install the `por` CLI
Clone the repo and install it globally with `npm`:
```shell
git clone git@github.com:mastoryberlin/porpoise.git
cd porpoise
npm i
npm add -g .
```
#### On Windows/WSL:
```shell
git clone git@github.com:mastoryberlin/porpoise.git
cd porpoise
npx tsc                              # produces dist/commands/por.js
chmod +x dist/commands/por.js
sudo npm i -g .                      # /usr prefix needs root
```

### Step 2: Prepare Your Project Repository
Porpoise assumes three things about your setup:
1) Your code is locally present as a *a bare git repository.
2) Your repo's *main branch* (`main`, `dev`, or whatever it's called in your case) is at the same time an Obsidian vault.
3) You are using GitHub and GitHub Projects to manage your issues, and have Orca connected with it as well.

#### "Bare" repository? What's that again?
A [bare repository](https://www.tomups.com/posts/git-worktrees/#worktrees-level-2-bare-repo) allows you to have *no* branch checked out in its root folder – or put differently, to have *all* your branches (including your main branch) live in one separate subfolder each. As a result, you get a local folder structure like this:

```sh
my-project
  .git # a simple text file pointing to main (or whatever your default branch is)
  main # worktree called like the branch it has checked out
  some-feature-branch # another worktree
```

While I personally prefer this setup, as a cleaner alternative to the more common one that nests all non-default feature branches in some git-ignored subfolder like (e.g. `my-project/worktrees`), it is especially useful to use Obsidian *only* on your default branch, while Orca deals with the feature branches.

The set this up, create a normal folder with a `.git` **text file** pointing at some subfolder which has your default branch checked out. In a nutshell, run these Bash commands, replacing `REPO` with your repository's name and `OWNER` with the repo owner (organization or GitHub user name):

```bash
mkdir REPO
cd REPO
git clone --bare git@github.com:OWNER/REPO .bare
echo "gitdir: ./.bare" > .git
git config remote.origin.fetch "+refs/heads/*:refs/remotes/origin/*"
git worktree add main # or whatever your repo's main branch is called
```

If you have multiple projects to work on with Porpoise (or even just with Orca or Obsidian), it is handy to create a script with the sequence above.
#### Make your repo an Obsidian vault
Once you're done with the git setup, open your project's *default branch* (!) in Obsidian (via Manage Vaults / Open Folder as Vault) to turn it into a vault. **Be sure NOT to open the repo's root folder itself** but **only** the default branch subfolder - e.g. open `main`, not `my-project`. (The [Vault Nickname Community Plugin](obsidian://show-plugin?id=vault-nickname) can help you avoid multiple vaults named `main` when dealing with multiple projects.) 

This creates a new `.obsidian` folder in your default branch to store your vault's local metadata. Consider adding a line `.obsidian` to your `.gitignore` file so it doesn't get committed together with the code!

#### Obtain a GitHub Personal Access Token (PAT)
Authorize the Porpoise CLI so it may create your GitHub issues and their status in a GitHub Project.
To this end, create a PAT from your GitHub account:
- go to your account settings (select "Settings" from your avatar's menu when logged into GitHub)
- select Developer Settings / Personal access tokens / Fine-grained tokens
- select whether the PAT is valid for all or just some select repositories, then give it minimal permissions:

### Step 3: Initialize the Project for Porpoise
```shell
cd path/to/my-project/main # or whatever your default branch is called
por init
```
The CLI will walk you through a number of questions. 

Afterwards, take a look at the new `porpoise-config.json` file generated in the worktree root, and check out the available config options which should be adjusted to your connected repo and GitHub project and mostly self-explanatory (at least if your editor supports JSON schema auto-complete and showing hints based on schema fields' `description` property, like VSCode does).
### Step 4: Configure Orca
1. Open Orca's Settings / Agents panel, pick any installed agent you don't actually use, *overwrite* i.e. customize its command line to `por agent`, and make it your new default agent. – Now, whenever you start a new agent session (from an issue or otherwise), you're defaulting to channel it through Porpoise which you can configure to delegate to any "real" agent of your choice via the `orca.agentCommands.newSession` config option.
2. In your project settings (or the defaults), look for the worktree creation / worktree archive hooks and set them to `por orca worktree setup` and `por orca worktree teardown`, respectively. Similar to the agent config above, this will make Orca channel hook handling through Porpoise, which in turn can be configured to run any commands or scripts committed with your code via the `orca.worktreeHooks.setup` / `orca.worktreeHooks.teardown` options.
### Step 5: Get the Obsidian Plugin (optional)
There's a community plugin available which adds 2 features that make working on a Porpoise project with Obsidian ultra-convenient:
1. Auto-completion of repo paths (default branch) after typing `@`. Typing Enter, Tab or / selects an entry; Ctrl+Backspace removes the last segment from a path. – Very useful to reference files to coding agents anywhere in prompts.
2. An integrated task graph, based on a slightly adjusted version of the [Spatial Task Graph community plugin](obsidian://show-plugin?id=spatial-task-graph). – The graph permits you to sketch tasks, break them down, and visualize their mutual dependencies, before elaborating them in detail.
The Obsidian plugin is great but hasn't yet been published to the community plugin registry, so you have to install it manually into your vault. If you have multiple projects hence multiple vaults, you'll have to repeat the steps below once for every vault (or tinker around with `mount` to replicate one common source folder into every vault's `plugins` folder).

First, clone the repo and build the source:
```shell
cd path/to/my/vault/
cd .obsidian/plugins
git clone git@github.com:mastoryberlin/porpoise-obsidian.git
cd porpoise-obsidian
npm i
npm run dev
```
This starts a "dev server", but you can immediately stop it via Ctrl+C.

Next, open your vault in Obsidian (you may have to close and reopen it for Obsidian to notice the plugin). Open Settings / Community Plugins, look for Porpoise, and activate it.

If everything worked, you'll see a new icon ![Pasted image 20261025174217.png](data:image/png;base64,) in the left sidebar. Click it to open the *task graph* - your entry hub to getting productive with Porpoise!
## How It Works
Here's a typical workflow as Porpoise encourages and supports it. 
Note how steps 1-3 are all possible without ever leaving Obsidian: Preparing your agent's context and specific task prompts is editing Markdown content, which is what Obsidian shines at - use speech-to-text, snippets, or any other plugins you want.
### 1) Prepare your tasks in prep files
- one task = one `# Markdown H1 header`
- organize tasks freely into any number of prep files in a dedicated folder.

```markdown
